<reason>A wins on the motion as written. B's cleverest moves — the selection-underperformance dilemma and the demand for equivalence bounds — cut against B's own position: the dilemma concedes observed parity (the motion's literal first-limb claim), and the equivalence-testing standard was exposed by A as one no family form or policy anywhere satisfies. A's decisive adaptation was turning B's own stepfamily example into proof that the research instruments detect policy-relevant family-structure gaps, making the convergent null on parental gender informative rather than empty; B never answered that inversion and also dropped A's US/UK convergence point, retreating to a "best-case environments" claim. On policy, A forced B to concede the practical content (custody, benefits, hospital access), and B's residual — don't encode parity as settled — was effectively framed as codified suspicion with real courtroom teeth. B's late biological-separation mechanism was genuinely responsive to A's Q1, but A neutralized it (shared with adoption, and those very children are inside the parity registries). B lands one real unanswered hit — A's tension between bracketing instability as a confounder and invoking "prior family transitions" as an offset — which, plus B's strong framing and a clipped opening, keeps this competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.1's inversion of B's stepfamily point: the same research tradition reliably detects divorce/stepfamily gaps, so whole-population registries finding nothing on parental gender are sensitive instruments returning a real zero — this defused B's core underpowered-null attack, and B never recovered it. Honorable mention to B2.2's catch of A's instability confounder/offset contradiction, A's clearest unanswered loss.</best_rebuttal>
